_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a4.1: What is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer? Rabba said: The verse states: “And if he will not redeem the field,” etc., “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee”: Rabbi Eliezer explains it and interprets it thus: “And if he will not redeem,” “it shall not be redeemed anymore”; “and if” the [Temple] treasurer “sold the field,” “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee” [shall be] for the priests. Conclude from this that if the treasurer did not sell the field, it does not go out to the priests.
rashi:a5.1: Does a sharp knife cut the verses?: They are not written that way; rather, they are written thus: “It shall not be redeemed anymore. But the field, when it goes out … for the priest,” which implies that once the Jubilee has arrived it may not be redeemed anymore, and it goes out to the priests even if the treasurer did not sell it.
rashi:a5.2: One might have thought it may not be redeemed: by the owner, even for it to be before him like a purchased field, like any other person who redeems it from the Temple treasury, from whose possession it goes out to the priests at the Jubilee.
rashi:a5.3: As it was: to be an ancestral field, so that it would not go out of his possession at the Jubilee; [in that way] it is not redeemed for him.
rashi:a7.1: It goes out to the priests: according to Rabbi Yehuda for money, and according to Rabbi Shimon for free; and in the end its owner can no longer redeem it at all.
rashi:a7.2: Is it not Rabbi Eliezer: who says that in the second [Jubilee cycle] too it is redeemable, if it was not redeemed in the first Jubilee.
rashi:a7.3: And the reason of Rabbi Eliezer is from here: since this “anymore” was needed to teach us that it is redeemable for him, to be before him like a purchased field, and this verse can be established only in the second Jubilee, conclude from this that in the second Jubilee it still stands to be redeemed.
rashi:a8.1: Which went out to the priests: where a person consecrated an ancestral field and another redeemed it, and it went out of his possession to the priests; and [the priest] consecrated it in the second Jubilee [cycle], and the owner came to redeem it from the treasurer. [Rashi describes the field as redeemed by another before it went to the priests; the Davidson English says only that the owner did not redeem it.]
rashi:a9.1: It might enter your mind to say it may not be redeemed: at all, since he did not redeem it from the first consecration, when he himself consecrated it.
rashi:a9.2: The verse states “anymore”: that it shall be before him like a purchased field, and when the Jubilee arrives it goes out of his possession and is divided among the priests.
rashi:a10.1: And similarly it is taught: [read it] as a plain statement, for we interpret [the verse] this way.
rashi:a10.2: In the Jubilee Year the field shall return: this is written about one who consecrates a purchased field, and this one redeemed it.
rashi:a10.3: The verse states: “To the one to whom the possession of the land belongs”: that is, the original owner, who sold it to the one who consecrated it.
rashi:a11.1: One might have thought it returns to the original owner: to the one who consecrated it in the first consecration, since “the possession of the land” is his.
rashi:a11.2: The verse states “to the one from whom it was bought”: and it was not bought from him; rather, it left his possession through consecration. Rather, it returns to the priest, from whom this buyer who consecrated it bought it. And this is also [the case] above: once the first one, for whom it was an ancestral field, consecrated it, and another redeemed it and it went out to the priests, it no longer returns to him unless he redeems it.
rashi:a12.1: And it was necessary to write “to the one from whom it was bought”: to teach us, as we said, that where one consecrated an ancestral field and did not redeem it, and another redeemed it and it went out to the priests, and a priest sold it in the second Jubilee [cycle], and the buyer consecrated it and another redeemed it, it does not return at the Jubilee to the first owner, who consecrated it originally.
rashi:a12.2: And it was necessary to write “it shall not be redeemed”: as we also established it above in this way: he consecrated it and another redeemed it and it went out to the priests, and a priest consecrated it; the first one can no longer redeem it to be before him like an ancestral field, since it went out from the first consecration to the priests.
rashi:a13.1: As it does not return at all: where a priest consecrated it, it never returns to anyone, since it was an ancestral field with respect to the priest, as it is written: “His ancestral possession shall be for the priest.” And when a priest consecrates it, it has the law of an ancestral field, and once another redeems it from the Temple treasury it goes out at the Jubilee and is divided among all the priests; to the priest who consecrated it, it returns only as a share like the rest of his brethren. And therefore it also does not return to the first owners to be before him like an ancestral field.
rashi:a13.2: But: where a priest sold it and the buyer consecrated it, it is now a purchased field; and when a person redeems it from the Temple treasury and the Jubilee arrives, it does not go out to the priests but returns. I would say it should return to its first owner, who consecrated it originally, since “the possession of the land” is his. [The verse] teaches us “to the one from whom it was bought,” that is, to the priest, from whom the last one who consecrated it bought it.
rashi:a14.1: It should remain in his hands: forever, like an ancestral field, and not go out to the priests at the Jubilee like a purchased field, like any other person who acquires an ancestral field from the Temple treasury, for whom it is a purchased field and from whom it goes out to the priests at the Jubilee.
rashi:a16.1: What was concluded about it: from where is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer?
rashi:a16.2: When it goes out: implies when it goes out of the hand of the one who redeemed it, according to the law of a person who buys land, which goes out at the Jubilee; with regard to that it says that it shall be for the priests. But its going out from the hand of the Temple treasury is not implied, for the verse has not yet taught us that consecrated property goes out at the Jubilee (by force of Temple maintenance).
tosafot:a5.1: What is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer: And if you say: but the plain sense of the verse is understood as Rabbi Eliezer holds: “And if he will not redeem the field,” the owner; “and if he sold,” that is, rather the treasurer sold it to another man; “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee” [shall be] for the priests. Evidently it goes out to the priests only when it was sold to another; but if another did not redeem it and it is still in the hand of the treasurer, then it does not go out to the priests. Evidently the plain sense of the verse is understood as Rabbi Eliezer holds [so why ask his reason]? But according to what I explained, that “and if he will not redeem” and “and if he sold” are two paths, this is fine, for it implies that in both of these it goes out to the priests.
tosafot:a6.1: If we say in the first Jubilee, why may it not be redeemed? It is also an ancestral field: This is puzzling: he should have said: If we say in the first Jubilee, but it is written: “And if he will indeed redeem the field … it shall be established for him” [Leviticus 27:19]! And perhaps that is what he means. And if you say: one can establish it in the first Jubilee, for example where another redeemed it from the treasurer and the owner redeemed it from him, for then the law is that it is like a purchased field and returns to the priests at the Jubilee, as we learned (above, Arakhin 25a): If another redeemed it, or one of the relatives, and he redeemed it from him, it goes out from under his hand at the Jubilee. One can say: it is not reasonable that the verse speaks of a redemption that comes from the hand of another to the hand of the owner, for the verse speaks only of redemption from the hand of the treasurer, since if another redeemed it, he will not sell it to the owner unless he wishes. And therefore “it shall not be redeemed anymore” speaks only of a redemption that comes from the hand of the treasurer.
gershom:a1.1: Rabbi Elazar says: They do not enter, and they do not give money to the Temple treasury; rather, it is called, etc. What is the reason of Rabbi Elazar? The verse states: “And if he will not redeem the field” [before] the Jubilee Year, “it shall not be redeemed anymore” by the owner; rather, it belongs to the Temple treasury, and [the priests] do not enter and do not give money. But “if he sold the field,” [that is, if] the treasurer [sold it] to another, after the Jubilee [comes] “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee,” shall be the priest’s. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads Rabbi Elazar throughout this discussion; the daf reads Rabbi Eliezer.]
gershom:a2.1: Abaye said: Does a sharp knife cut the verses?: That is, this one attaches “it shall not be redeemed” to what is before it, to “and if he will not redeem,” and attaches “But the field” to what is before it, to “and if he sold.” Who cut them and separated them?
gershom:a3.1: Rather, Abaye said: The reason of Rabbi Elazar is as it is taught: “It shall not be redeemed”; one might have thought it may not be redeemed after the Jubilee so as to be before him to redeem, even as a purchased field, so that it is his until the Jubilee and returns to the Temple treasury at the Jubilee.
gershom:a4.1: The verse states “anymore”: that is, after it went out at the Jubilee, it may no longer be redeemed so that its law is again as it was, like an ancestral field that returns to its owner at the Jubilee; but it is redeemable for him as a purchased field, so that it is his until the Jubilee Year, and at the Jubilee it returns to the Temple treasury. For once the Jubilee arrived and it was not redeemed, the Temple treasury acquired it; when this one goes back and redeems it from the Temple treasury, he is like a buyer. And it is written: “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee … his ancestral possession shall be for the priest”; “In the Jubilee Year the field shall return to the one from whom it was bought,” and that is the Temple treasury. And he infers: when does it apply, [that it says] “but it is redeemable to be before him like a purchased field”? If we say in the first Jubilee, when the Jubilee Year has not yet arrived, why does it say that it is not redeemable as it was? Why not? It still has the law of an ancestral field, since the Jubilee has not yet passed.
gershom:a5.1: Rather, it is obvious [that it refers to] the second Jubilee: [that is where] the tanna of the baraita stands, [and according to whom does he teach the baraita:] “but it is redeemable to be before him like a purchased field,” that is, it returns to the Temple treasury.
gershom:a6.1: If according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, it goes out to the priests: even from the first Jubilee, as we learned: The priests enter into it, one Sage as he holds and the other Sage as he holds. And once it has gone out to the priests, it is no longer redeemable from them by the measure of a ḥomer of barley for fifty shekels of silver, but [only] at its value, whether among the orchards of Sebaste or in the sandy soil of the district.
gershom:a7.1: Rather, is it not: since it teaches “redeemable,” which implies for fifty shekels, conclude from this that it is stated according to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that it belonged to the Temple treasury at the first Jubilee.
gershom:a8.1: And can you understand it as you have resolved it?: Granted, according to Rabbi Elazar, who says it belongs to the Temple treasury, this “anymore” is [fine] as you said: “it shall not be redeemed anymore,” that is, it is redeemable for fifty shekels, as it still belongs to the Temple treasury.
gershom:a9.1: But according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, who say: it belongs to the priests, what do they interpret from this “anymore”? It is not redeemable at all for fifty shekels, only at its value; if so, what does this “anymore” teach us?
gershom:a10.1: Rather, what are we dealing with here: The baraita [speaks] of a field that went out to the priests, as [Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon] hold, and it went out to the priests; and afterward a priest consecrated it, [or] one priest [consecrated] his share, or the [priestly] family consecrated all of it. Since it came into the hand of the Temple treasury, it is redeemable for fifty shekels of silver, and the owner came to redeem it. It might enter your mind to say: since it has [already] gone out to the priests, it shall no longer go out to the hand of the owner, even as a purchased field. The verse states “anymore”: as it was, as an ancestral field, it is not redeemable to belong to the owner, but it is redeemable to be before him like a purchased field, and it returns [to the priests] at the Jubilee. And we have still not heard the reason of Rabbi Elazar.
gershom:a11.1: In the Jubilee Year the field shall return: this is written about a purchased field. “To the one from whom it was bought”: one might have thought even to the treasurer from whom he bought it; that is, if he had a purchased field and consecrated it, and then bought it back from the treasurer, when the Jubilee arrives one might have thought the field returns to the treasurer from whom he bought it, since we can read of it “to the one from whom it was bought.” The verse states: “To the one to whom the possession of the land belongs.”
gershom:a12.1: It returns to the first seller, for a person cannot consecrate an item that is not his, and not to the treasurer. [The printed text marks this note and the opening of the next as an added passage.]
gershom:a13.1: Let it state “to the one to whom the possession of the land belongs,” and it would not need “to the one from whom it was bought”; why does the verse state “to the one from whom it was bought”? Rather, [it is needed] for a field that went out to the priests, and a priest sold it, and the buyer consecrated it, and another redeemed it. One might have thought: since another redeemed it and the buyer did not redeem it, and it goes out of the hand of this one who redeemed it and returns at the Jubilee, since there is so much returning here, that it came into the hand of a third person, one might have thought it returns to the original owners. The verse states “to the one from whom it was bought,” that is, it returns to the hand of the priest who sold it, and not to the owners. And this is a support [for the view] that it returns to the priests.
gershom:a14.1: And it was necessary to write “it shall not be redeemed” and “to the one from whom it was bought,” to learn from both of them that it returns to the priests and not to the owners. For if [it had written] only “it shall not be redeemed,” I would have said: what is the reason it does not return to the owners at the Jubilee? Because “it shall not be redeemed” is written of it, for it does not return at all, since it left the owners’ domain and returns to the priests, and there is not so much returning here; and furthermore, “shall return” is not written in that verse. But here, where it does return, as “the field shall return” is written of it, and furthermore there is much returning here, since it came into the hand of a third person: since it returns, as it is written “shall return,” I would say it should return to the owners. Therefore it is written “to the one from whom it was bought,” to the priest who sold it.
gershom:a15.1: And if it had written only “to the one from whom it was bought,” as we explained, where a priest sold it and the buyer consecrated it and another redeemed it, [I would say] that is why it does not return to the owners: because the owners did not give money to the treasurer; rather, another redeemed it. But here, in this “it shall not be redeemed anymore” that we discussed above, where a priest consecrated it and the owners came to redeem it, since the owners give [money], I would say it should remain in their domain.
gershom:a16.1: The Merciful One wrote “it shall not be redeemed”: that it does not return to the owners.
gershom:a17.1: What was concluded about it: for we still do not know the reason of Rabbi Elazar, who said above: The priests do not enter until another redeems it.
gershom:a18.1: Rava said: Because the verse states: “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee”: for it could have said: “But the field in the Jubilee shall be holy for the Lord,” etc. What is [taught by] “when it goes out”? It teaches us that when it goes out of the hand of another, who redeemed it from the hand of the treasurer [before] the Jubilee [or] bought it from the treasurer, then “his ancestral possession shall be for the priest.”
rashi:b1.1: A dilemma was raised before them: according to Rabbi Eliezer, who says that in the second Jubilee [cycle] it is redeemable if it was not redeemed in the first.
rashi:b1.2: Is the owner in the second Jubilee like another: so that if he redeems it, it goes out of his possession to the priests?
rashi:b1.3: Or not: are they not like another; rather, just as, had he redeemed it in the first Jubilee [cycle], it would remain in his possession, now too it remains in his possession?
rashi:b4.1: It goes out to the priests: and in the second Jubilee [cycle] it is not redeemable at all.
rashi:b14.1: Mishna. One who purchases a field from his father and his father died, etc., it is like an ancestral field: since before he consecrated it, it fell to him by inheritance. Therefore, if he comes to redeem it, he redeems [it at] fifty sela per beit kor, like an ancestral field; and if he did not redeem it and another redeemed it, it goes out to the priests at the Jubilee.
rashi:b14.2: Like a purchased field: for we go by the time when he consecrated it. Therefore, if he comes to redeem it, he redeems it at its value, according to the law of a purchased field; and if he did not redeem it and another redeemed it, it returns to him at the Jubilee, since at the time he consecrated it the land itself was not his, as it was due to return to his father at the Jubilee like other sales. And he is like anyone else who consecrates a purchased field: whoever redeems it from the treasurer returns it at the Jubilee “to the one to whom the possession of the land belongs,” that is, his father, and this one inherits his father’s right.
rashi:b16.1: A purchased field: that one consecrated and another redeemed does not go out to the priests at the Jubilee, but [returns] to the one who sold it to the one who consecrated it.
rashi:b16.2: For a person cannot consecrate an item that is not his: and this land was his only until the Jubilee.
rashi:b16.3: May always consecrate: this is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b16.4: And may always redeem: if a priest consecrated the land of his inheritance, he may redeem it even after the Jubilee, as it is written: “The Levites shall have a perpetual right of redemption” (Leviticus 25:32).
rashi:b19.1: Gemara. Rabbi Meir holds that acquisition of the produce: that it was acquired by the son in his father’s lifetime for the produce, to eat the produce, and not for [the land] itself, since it was due to return at the Jubilee, is like acquisition of the land itself. Therefore, when his father died before he consecrated it, had the verse not taught us that it is like an ancestral field, I would have said it is not an ancestral field, since even without his father’s death it was acquired by him; therefore a verse was necessary for this. But if he consecrated it while it was still a purchased field and afterward his father died, the verse does not include it for us as an ancestral field; rather, it is a purchased field.
rashi:b19.2: And Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon hold that it is not like acquisition of the land itself: and when his father died before he consecrated it, he inherits the land itself, and it is an ancestral field. Therefore a verse was not necessary to include this case, since it is a full ancestral field, for in his father’s lifetime it was not acquired by him. And the verse comes for [the case where] he consecrated it and afterward his father died: even though at the time of consecration it was a purchased field, now that his father died before the redemption, it is an ancestral field.
rashi:b21.1: Is like acquisition of the land itself: and so for [the case where] his father died and afterward he consecrated it, a verse is also necessary.
tosafot:b1.1: A dilemma was raised before them: Is the owner in the second Jubilee [like another]? Explanation: according to Rabbi Eliezer, are they like another or not? For since it was not redeemed and was not divided among the priests at the Jubilee, as it is still in the hand of the treasurer, the owners can redeem it. For what is written, “it shall not be redeemed anymore,” which we interpret to mean that it is not redeemed [to be] as it was, refers to where another redeemed it from the treasurer; but where it was never divided among the priests, the verse “it shall not be redeemed anymore” does not speak of that, and it should remain in the hand of the owners when they redeem it from the treasurer.
tosafot:b5.1: Rather, what are we dealing with here? With a field that went out to the priests: Explanation: for example, an ancestral field that its owners consecrated and another redeemed before the Jubilee, which goes out to the priests at the Jubilee; and the priest to whom that field fell came and consecrated it, and this is in the second Jubilee [cycle], and the owners came to redeem it. For it might enter your mind, if only “it shall not be redeemed” were written, that he may not redeem it to be before him even like a purchased field. The verse states “anymore”: as it was, it is not redeemed, [but it is redeemed] to be like a purchased field, meaning that it returns to the priests at the Jubilee. And now “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee,” etc., refers to the two paths the verse speaks of, both “and if he will not redeem the field” and “and if he sold the field to another man,” for the verse in fact speaks of two matters, as I explained above. And if so, according to Rabbi Eliezer too this is the explanation of the verse; and above he asks: What is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer? And he concludes: What was concluded about it, (that is, what is the reason) of Rabbi Eliezer? Rava said: The verse states: “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee,” etc., “when it goes out” from under the hand of another. Explanation: for “when it goes out” implies that it goes out of the hand of another who redeemed it from the hand of the treasurer; but as long as it is in the hand of the treasurer, it does not go out at the Jubilee.
tosafot:b16.1: A purchased field does not go out to the priests at the Jubilee, for a person cannot consecrate an item that is not his: At first glance it implies [that this is] where another redeemed it from the treasurer before the Jubilee. And Rashi explained in his commentary on the Torah that even if another did not redeem it, but it is still in the hand of the treasurer, it goes out for free at the Jubilee to the original owners, “to whom the possession of the land belongs.”
tosafot:b20.1: According to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, acquisition of the produce is like acquisition of the land itself, etc.: I explained it in [the chapter] HaSholei’aḥ (Gittin 48a).
gershom:b1.1: The owners redeemed it in the second Jubilee: according to Rabbi Elazar, are the owners like another, so that it again goes out to the priests, or are they not like [a case where] another redeemed it?
gershom:b2.1: Come and hear: “It shall not be redeemed anymore,” etc. Rather, it is obvious [that it refers to] the second Jubilee, and it is redeemable to be before him like a purchased field, which returns to the priests at the Jubilee, as it is written: “Shall be for the priest,” etc. Evidently the owners in the second Jubilee are like another.
gershom:b3.1: And can you understand it, etc.: and he rejects it, [saying] that the reason cannot be learned from here.
gershom:b4.1: What was concluded about it? Rava said: Come and hear: for we learned a baraita explicitly that they are like another: Rabbi Eliezer says, etc. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text has “Rava said” here; the daf reads only “Come and hear.”]
gershom:b5.1: If from the mishna, I would have said, etc.: the baraita teaches us that they are not like another.
gershom:b6.1: Excluding this, which is fit to become an ancestral field: for since, had he not bought it, it would have fallen to him by inheritance and been an ancestral field, now too, even though he consecrated it and afterward his father died, it is an ancestral field.
gershom:b7.1: One who consecrates a purchased field and did not redeem it, it does not go out to the priests at the Jubilee, for a person cannot consecrate an item that is not his: for it is the seller’s ancestral possession, and it returns to him at the Jubilee.
gershom:b8.1: Rabbi Meir holds that acquisition of the produce is like acquisition of the land itself.
gershom:b9.1: For one who buys a field from his father has, in his father’s lifetime, only the produce, and Rabbi Meir holds that acquisition of the produce is like acquisition of the land itself. Therefore, when he consecrated it in his father’s lifetime, it is like a purchased field: just as the produce is his, so he acquired the land itself, and it is no longer fit to be his ancestral field; rather, it has the law of a purchased field.
gershom:b10.1: And Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon hold: acquisition of the produce is not like acquisition of the land itself. Therefore they say it is like an ancestral field, since it is fit to be an ancestral field.
gershom:b11.1: In general: everywhere, with regard to one who wrote all his property over to his son [to take effect] after his death, [where] neither of them can sell; that is, according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, acquisition of the produce is like acquisition of the land itself. And here [they derive it from] a superfluous verse.
